trial.title: A Brief Intervention for Cannabis Use

endpoints.description: The TLFB is a calendar based assessment that is able to capture the frequency and quantity of substance use and other measurable behaviors. Responders identify anchor dates to facilitate recall of days in which substances were used.

This is a 23-item assessment of the frequency in which problems or negative consequences associated with cannabis use have occurred. For each item, participants select 0 times, 1-2 times, 3-5 times, 6-10 times, or 10+ times in the past month. Higher scores on this inventory indicate a higher frequency of problems or consequences experienced.

endpoints.measure: Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI) Cannabis Use Disorder Module
endpoints.description: This is a 12-item semi-structured clinician interview that assesses diagnostic symptom criteria of cannabis use disorder (CUD) from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th Edition (DSM-5). Clinicians select either 'yes' or 'no' for the presence of the symptom.

This is a relatively brief objective assessment of recent cannabis use that is collected through mouth swab and is tested at Forensic Fluids Laboratory for the presence of delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), delta-8 THC, and cannabidiol (CBD) using a cut-off of 1 nanogram/liter.

value.effect_measure: mean difference in cannabis use days (TLFB)
value.estimand: Bloom vs Health Education at 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat
value.uncertainty: Pilot trial with no direct Bloom efficacy data; wide confidence intervals due to small sample (n=62) and indirect evidence base
value.rationale: Brief values-based interventions for cannabis in emerging adults typically reduce use days by 2-5 days versus minimal/health education controls. Bloom's personalized feedback and values-alignment approach should outperform generic health education. Small pilot sample limits precision.

value.effect_measure: mean difference in MAPI total score
value.estimand: Bloom vs Health Education at 3-month follow-up
value.uncertainty: MAPI scores correlate with use frequency but pilot trial lacks power for precise estimation; no direct validation in brief intervention trials
value.rationale: Cannabis-related problems measured by MAPI should decrease as use frequency declines. Expected moderate correlation with TLFB outcomes. Health education control may show minimal change in problems.

value.estimand: Bloom vs Health Education at 6-month follow-up
value.uncertainty: CUD remission requires sustained abstinence/reduction; brief 2-session intervention may be insufficient for full remission in frequent users; pilot underpowered for this binary outcome
value.rationale: MINI CUD module assesses DSM-5 criteria. Brief interventions rarely produce high remission rates in frequent cannabis users. Small between-group difference expected due to limited intervention intensity.

value.estimand: Bloom vs Health Education at 1-month follow-up
value.uncertainty: Oral fluid detection window (24-48 hours) shorter than TLFB recall; may not capture all use days; high baseline use makes complete negativity unlikely
value.rationale: Objective biospecimen should correlate with self-reported reduction but detection limitations and high baseline use frequency mean most participants remain positive. Modest between-group difference expected.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06395389 is a pilot randomized trial comparing Bloom (values-based brief intervention) vs Health Education (active comparator) for emerging adults (18-25 years) with frequent cannabis use. Primary endpoint: TLFB measuring cannabis use days. Secondary endpoints: MAPI (problems), MINI CUD diagnosis, oral fluid biospecimen.

Evidence base: Europe PMC search returned studies on cannabis brief interventions for young adults. Key findings: (1) Mobile interventions show modest reductions in cannabis use frequency; (2) Brief motivational interventions typically achieve small-to-moderate effect sizes for substance use reduction in emerging adults; (3) Health education controls often show minimal change or slight placebo effects.

Evidence-role assessment: No direct numeric evidence for this specific trial (Bloom vs HealthEdu). Indirect evidence from similar populations supports direction of effect (reduction in use days) but not precise magnitude. Mismatch: other interventions differ in modality (mobile vs in-person), duration, and theoretical framework.

Primary endpoint (TLFB): Brief interventions for cannabis in emerging adults typically show 2-5 day reduction in use days over 1-3 months vs minimal intervention controls. Values-based approaches (ACT-informed) may show comparable or slightly better outcomes than health education. Predict modest reduction favoring Bloom.
Secondary-0 (MAPI): Problems/consequences correlate with use frequency. Expected reduction parallels TLFB changes. Small-to-moderate effect anticipated.
Secondary-1 (MINI CUD): Diagnosis remission rates in brief intervention trials for cannabis vary widely (10-35%). Pilot trial likely underpowered for definitive CUD remission endpoint.

Secondary-2 (Oral fluid): Objective biomarker correlates with self-reported use but detection window (hours-days) shorter than TLFB recall period. Expected concordance with self-report trends but higher variability.

Key uncertainties: (1) Pilot design limits power; (2) No published Bloom-specific efficacy data; (3) Health education as active comparator may attenuate between-group differences; (4) Retention in emerging adult cannabis trials variable (60-80%).
Safety: Behavioral interventions have minimal adverse event risk. No serious safety signals anticipated.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06395389 is a pilot randomized trial comparing Bloom (values-based brief intervention) vs Health Education (active comparator) for emerging adults (18-25 years) with frequent cannabis use. Primary endpoint: TLFB measuring cannabis use days. Secondary endpoints: MAPI (problems), MINI CUD diagnosis, oral fluid biospecimen.

Evidence base: Europe PMC search returned studies on cannabis brief interventions for young adults. Key findings: (1) Mobile interventions show modest reductions in cannabis use frequency; (2) Brief motivational interventions typically achieve small-to-moderate effect sizes for substance use reduction in emerging adults; (3) Health education controls often show minimal change or slight placebo effects.

Evidence-role assessment: No direct numeric evidence for this specific trial (Bloom vs HealthEdu). Indirect evidence from similar populations supports direction of effect (reduction in use days) but not precise magnitude. Mismatch: other interventions differ in modality (mobile vs in-person), duration, and theoretical framework.

Primary endpoint (TLFB): Brief interventions for cannabis in emerging adults typically show 2-5 day reduction in use days over 1-3 months vs minimal intervention controls. Values-based approaches (ACT-informed) may show comparable or slightly better outcomes than health education. Predict modest reduction favoring Bloom.
Secondary-0 (MAPI): Problems/consequences correlate with use frequency. Expected reduction parallels TLFB changes. Small-to-moderate effect anticipated.
Secondary-1 (MINI CUD): Diagnosis remission rates in brief intervention trials for cannabis vary widely (10-35%). Pilot trial likely underpowered for definitive CUD remission endpoint.

Secondary-2 (Oral fluid): Objective biomarker correlates with self-reported use but detection window (hours-days) shorter than TLFB recall period. Expected concordance with self-report trends but higher variability.

Key uncertainties: (1) Pilot design limits power; (2) No published Bloom-specific efficacy data; (3) Health education as active comparator may attenuate between-group differences; (4) Retention in emerging adult cannabis trials variable (60-80%).
Safety: Behavioral interventions have minimal adverse event risk. No serious safety signals anticipated.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06395389 is a pilot randomized trial comparing Bloom (values-based brief intervention) vs Health Education for emerging adults (18-25) with frequent cannabis use. Sample size n=62 estimated. Primary endpoint TLFB measures cannabis use frequency/quantity. Secondary endpoints include MAPI (problems), MINI (CUD diagnosis), and oral fluid THC. Evidence from motivational interviewing meta-analyses (Calomarde-Gomez et al.) shows MI reduces cannabis use and achieves abstinence in adults. Brief interventions for cannabis in emerging adults show modest effect sizes (g≈0.2-0.4) for use reduction. As a pilot trial, primary goal is feasibility and preliminary efficacy signals. Bloom's values-based approach aligns with MI principles suggesting potential superiority over health education. Expected TLFB reduction: Bloom 20-30% greater than Health Education. Expected MAPI reduction: small-to-moderate favoring Bloom. MINI CUD remission: modest rates favoring Bloom. Oral fluid: biochemical verification expected to correlate with self-report.

Published: August 21, 2026 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0355941 Article Authors Metrics Comments Media Coverage Peer Review Reader Comments Figures Figures Abstract Background Cannabis use disorder (CUD) imposes a significant global health burden, yet comparative evidence for the diverse range of non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs) remains fragmented. Existing reviews often combine diverse NPIs into broad categories, overlooking the specific contributions of neurobiological modalities. This study aims to establish a comprehensive comparative efficacy hierarchy for non-pharmacological CUD interventions by integrating psychosocial therapies and neurotherapy into a unified analytical framework. Methods We will conduct a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials comparing NPIs against control group(including waitlist, no-intervention, or non-specific control) or another NPIs for individuals with CUD. Systematic searches will be performed across PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL). Primary benefit outcomes will include biochemically verified cannabis abstinenc and self-reported days of cannabis use over the past 30 days. Primary acceptability will be evaluated by treatment retention, defined using an intention-to-treat approach as the proportion of randomized participants completing at least one session during the final treatment week, alongside follow-up retention rates. Primary safety will be assessed by the overall incidence of intervention-related adverse and serious adverse events. Pairs of reviewers will independently perform study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias. A frequentist NMA will be conducted to synthesize evidence. We will employ the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluations(GRADE) approach to assess the certainty of evidence and categorize interventions using a minimally contextualized framework based on predefined decision thresholds. Results Comprehensive search strategies have been validated across target databases. Formal study screening, data extraction, quantitative network meta-analyses, and GRADE evidence assessments are scheduled for completion by September 2026, followed by final manuscript preparation. Conclusion This NMA will establish a comprehensive comparative evidence hierarchy for non-pharmacological CUD interventions by bridging psychosocial and neurobiological modalities. By pairing network estimates with GRADE certainty assessments, our findings will offer a standardized, actionable foundation for tailored clinical care and future trial methodology. analysis_trace: Trial NCT06395389 is a pilot randomized trial comparing Bloom (values-based brief intervention) vs Health Education for emerging adults (18-25) with frequent cannabis use. Sample size n=62 estimated. Primary endpoint TLFB measures cannabis use frequency/quantity. Secondary endpoints include MAPI (problems), MINI (CUD diagnosis), and oral fluid THC. Evidence from motivational interviewing meta-analyses (Calomarde-Gomez et al.) shows MI reduces cannabis use and achieves abstinence in adults. Brief interventions for cannabis in emerging adults show modest effect sizes (g≈0.2-0.4) for use reduction. As a pilot trial, primary goal is feasibility and preliminary efficacy signals. Bloom's values-based approach aligns with MI principles suggesting potential superiority over health education. Expected TLFB reduction: Bloom 20-30% greater than Health Education.
